context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.

audio.t: Hi, I was hoping to reserve a study room for Thursday evening.
Let me check. The rooms on the second floor are all booked, but there's one in the basement open from six to eight.
The basement? Is it quiet down there? I'm practicing a presentation, so I'll be talking out loud.
That's actually perfect. The basement rooms are soundproofed, and each one has a whiteboard.
Great. There will be four of us. Is that okay?
Each room holds up to six people. I'll just need your student ID to book it.
Oh no, I left my wallet in my dorm. Can I give you the number instead?
Sure, that works. Go ahead and read it to me.

qs.q: Why does the student want a study room?
choices: To study quietly by herself
To meet with a tutor
To practice a presentation with a group
To use the whiteboard for math problems
qs.explain: She says she is practicing a presentation and that four people will come.

qs.q: What problem does the student have?
choices: She wants a room for more than six people.
She does not have her student ID with her.
The basement room is too far away.
She cannot come on Thursday.
qs.explain: She left her wallet in her dorm, so she offers to read out the number.

context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the registrar's office.

audio.t: Hello, I'd like to drop my statistics course, but the online system won't let me.

Will I still get a refund?
Unfortunately, no. After the deadline, tuition for that class isn't refunded.
Okay. I'd still rather have a W than fail the course. What do I need to do?
Fill out this form and get your professor's signature. Then bring it back by next Friday.
Can I email it instead?
The form has to be turned in here, in person.

choices: The system is not working today.
He owes money to the university.
His professor has not approved it.
The deadline for dropping has passed.
qs.explain: The staff member says the online drop deadline was last Friday.

qs.q: What will the student most likely do next?
choices: Ask for a refund
Switch to a different statistics section
Get his professor to sign the form
Email the form to the registrar
qs.explain: He must get a signature and deliver the form in person. No refund is possible and email is not allowed.

Email the paper as a PDF before noon on Thursday

Go back to the health center on Thursday

Then here's a thought. Could the internship be done part time, or remotely?

choices: It is on a noisy floor.
It is far from the dining hall.
It will not be available until next semester.
It costs more.

context: Listen to a conversation between a student and an information technology help desk worker.

audio.t: Hi, I can't connect my laptop to the campus Wi-Fi. It keeps asking for my password, and then it fails.

Makes sense. Thanks. Do I need to do anything else?
No, but if it still doesn't work, bring it by tomorrow. We're open until five.

choices: The campus network is down.
Her account was locked.
Her laptop saved her old password.
Her laptop is too old.
qs.explain: The worker says the laptop is still trying the old password.

choices: It uses a different network.
It updated the saved password automatically.
It has a stronger signal.
She has never changed the phone's settings.
qs.explain: He explains that phones often update saved passwords after signing in to email.

context: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.

audio.t: So last time we noticed that the Moon always shows the same face to Earth. Today I want to explain why, because it isn't a coincidence. The effect is called tidal locking. Here's the idea. Earth's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, so the Moon gets stretched slightly, a bit like a lemon. Early in its history, the Moon was spinning faster than it does now.

As it spun, that stretched bulge kept being carried out of line with Earth, and Earth's gravity tugged on the bulge to pull it back. That tugging worked like a brake. Over millions of years, the spin slowed until one rotation took exactly as long as one orbit. At that point, the bulge stayed pointed at Earth, and the braking stopped.

Now, you might wonder if this is rare. It isn't. Most large moons in our solar system are tidally locked to their planets. Even Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, always face each other, which means each one is locked to the other.

qs.q: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: Why the Moon always shows the same side to Earth
How the Moon was formed
Why the Moon is shaped like a lemon
How tides are created on Earth
qs.explain: The professor explains tidal locking as the reason for the Moon's constant face.

qs.q: What acted like a brake on the Moon's spin?
choices: Friction from the Moon's surface
The pull of other planets
The Moon's own orbit slowing down
Earth's gravity pulling on the Moon's bulge
qs.explain: Earth tugged on the bulge, which slowed the rotation.

qs.q: Why does the professor mention Pluto and Charon?
choices: To show that moons can lose their locking
To show that tidal locking is common
To compare the sizes of moons and planets
To explain how Pluto was discovered
qs.explain: The example supports the claim that tidal locking is not rare.

qs.q: What can be inferred about a moon that spins much faster than it orbits?

It is too small to be affected by gravity.
It will soon leave its orbit.
qs.explain: Since braking only stops once rotation matches the orbit, a faster spin suggests the process is unfinished.

context: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

audio.t: Let's talk about something that happens underground, where most of us never look. Many trees form partnerships with fungi. The fungus grows thin threads around the tree's roots and even into them. These threads reach much farther into the soil than roots can, so they bring water and minerals, such as phosphorus, to the tree. In return, the tree gives the fungus sugars that it makes through photosynthesis.

What surprised researchers was that one fungal network can connect several trees at once. In one experiment, scientists shaded a young tree so it couldn't photosynthesize well. Later, they found that carbon had moved to it from taller neighbors through the fungus. Some people call this the wood wide web.

Now, I should add a note of caution. We don't yet know whether trees send carbon on purpose, to help each other, or whether it simply flows from places with a lot to places with little. The experiments show movement. They don't show intention. So be careful when you read headlines that say trees talk to each other.

qs.explain: The tree provides sugars made through photosynthesis.

context: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

audio.t: Here's a question for you. If you have ten hours to study for an exam, is it better to study all ten the night before, or to spread them over two weeks? Psychologists have tested this for more than a century, and the answer is consistent. Spreading it out wins. This is called the spacing effect.

In a classic study, students learned word lists either in one long session or in several short ones with breaks in between. A week later, the group that studied in several sessions remembered far more words. Researchers think that each time you return to material, you have to pull it out of memory, and that effort strengthens the memory.

Interestingly, students often feel that cramming works better. After a long session, the material feels familiar, so they think they know it. But familiarity isn't the same as knowledge. That false confidence is one reason many people keep cramming, even though it works worse.

qs.explain: The spacing effect favors spreading study time out.

context: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.

audio.t: Imagine you buy a movie ticket for twelve dollars. Twenty minutes in, you realize the film is terrible. Do you stay or leave? Many people stay, because they paid for the ticket. Economists call this the sunk cost fallacy. A sunk cost is money or effort that has already been spent and can't be recovered, no matter what you decide next.

The key point is this. Since the twelve dollars is gone either way, it shouldn't affect your decision. What should matter is the future. Would the next ninety minutes be better spent watching this movie or doing something else? If something else is more enjoyable, you should leave.

This applies far beyond movies. A company may keep funding a failing project because it has already invested millions. A student may stay in a major they dislike because they've already completed two years. In both cases, the past investment is pulling on the decision, when only future costs and benefits should count.
To be fair, there's one exception. Sometimes continuing is rational because quitting has its own costs, such as a penalty fee. But that is a future cost, not a sunk one.

qs.explain: The professor defines the sunk cost fallacy and explains how to avoid it.

qs.explain: Only future costs and benefits should count.

context: Listen to part of a talk in a history class.

audio.t: When Johannes Gutenberg introduced movable type printing in Germany in the fourteen forties, books became cheaper almost overnight. Before that, every book was copied by hand, which could take a scribe months. Within fifty years, printers had produced millions of books across Europe.

You might assume that cheaper books immediately made everyone literate. That didn't happen. For a long time, most people still couldn't read, and printers mostly sold to universities, churches, and wealthy merchants. What changed first was not how many people could read, but how fast ideas could travel.

A good example is Martin Luther's writings. Within a few weeks of publication, his pamphlets were being read in cities hundreds of miles away. Earlier, such a message might have taken years to spread, if it spread at all. Printers also helped standardize spelling, since they wanted their books to be understood in different regions.

context: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.

audio.t: If you've ever walked from a park into a busy downtown on a summer afternoon, you've probably felt it. Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them. This is called the urban heat island effect. There are three main causes. First, dark surfaces like asphalt and rooftops absorb more sunlight than grass or soil does.
Second, cities have fewer plants. Plants cool the air by releasing water vapor, a bit like sweating. Third, buildings and cars give off heat directly, from air conditioners, engines, and so on.

So what can be done? Some cities paint rooftops white, which reflects sunlight. Others plant trees along streets. In Los Angeles, a program used a light gray coating on certain roads, and surface temperatures dropped. But these methods help only so much, since the heat from air conditioning is hard to reduce.

context: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.

audio.t: Let's consider what happens when people with no shared language have to communicate regularly, such as traders or workers on plantations. They often develop a pidgin, a simplified language with limited vocabulary, borrowed mostly from one of the languages, and very little grammar. A pidgin isn't anyone's first language. It's a tool for specific purposes.

Here's where it gets fascinating. When children grow up hearing a pidgin as their main input, something remarkable happens. They don't just copy it. They expand it, adding consistent grammar, such as ways to mark tense and plurals. The result is called a creole, which is a full language with native speakers.

Haitian Creole is one example. Its vocabulary mostly comes from French, but its grammar developed in its own way and is different from French. Some linguists argue that this shows children have a natural ability to build grammar, even when the input they receive is incomplete.

context: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.

audio.t: Look at the painting on the screen, a religious scene from the thirteen hundreds. Notice how flat it seems. The figures are lined up across the front, the buildings don't recede, and sizes depend on importance, not distance. Now compare it with a painting from the fourteen twenties. Suddenly we feel we could walk into the scene. What changed?

The answer is linear perspective, a technique developed by the architect Filippo Brunelleschi in Florence. The idea is that parallel lines, like the edges of a road or a tiled floor, appear to meet at a single point in the distance, called the vanishing point. By drawing lines that way, artists could create a convincing illusion of depth.

Brunelleschi was an architect, not a painter, so he approached the problem mathematically. His friend Alberti then wrote down the rules in a book, which allowed other artists to learn them. That's a big reason the technique spread so quickly through Italy.

context: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.

audio.t: On a hike in the northern United States, you might come across a huge boulder sitting alone in a field, made of a completely different type of rock from everything around it. Geologists call these boulders erratics. They aren't from here. So how did a boulder the size of a house get to the middle of farmland?

The answer is glaciers. During the last ice age, sheets of ice thousands of feet thick moved slowly across the land. As they advanced, they picked up rocks, from pebbles to boulders, frozen into the ice. When the climate warmed and the ice melted, it dropped them, sometimes hundreds of miles from where they started.

Erratics are useful to geologists because by identifying the rock type, they can trace where it came from. That tells us the direction the ice moved. For example, boulders of a distinctive red rock found in one state matched a cliff far to the north, which showed that the ice had traveled southward.

The rocks were left behind.
qs.explain: The ice dropped the rocks.

choices: To explain why some rocks are colored

To show that glaciers melt slowly
To compare different ice ages
qs.explain: The red rock matched a cliff to the north, showing that ice moved south.

context: Listen to part of a talk in a physiology class.

audio.t: Many of you pulled an all-nighter last semester, so this might hurt. Sleep doesn't just rest the brain. It actively helps store what you learned during the day. Researchers have found that during deep sleep, the brain replays patterns of activity that occurred while we were awake, almost like rehearsing.

In one study, two groups of participants learned a list of word pairs in the evening. One group slept normally, and the other stayed awake all night. After that, both groups got two full nights of recovery sleep, and then they were tested. You would expect no difference, right? But the group that slept the first night remembered more.

This suggests that sleep soon after learning is important, and that you can't completely make up for it later. So if you have an exam on Friday, the sleep you get on Wednesday night matters too, not just the sleep on Thursday.
